Topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): From Chaos to Order

Target audience: University students (Introductory Statistics)

Section: section_1 — Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions

Lecture lines:
Data shapes aren't always bell-shaped.
Some distributions are uniform or skewed.
Most real-world data is messy.

Planned animations:
1. Show two distinct data containers: a 'Flat' box (Uniform) and a 'Mountain' curve (Normal). 2. Label 'Flat' as #FF5733 (Uniform) and 'Mountain' as #33FF57 (Normal). 3. Animate a 'messy' scattered cloud of points turning into these shapes. 4. Highlight 'Real-world data' text in #FFFFFF to emphasize it is often unpredictable. 5. Conclude with both shapes side-by-side.
1. Show an acorn icon popping up into the scene. 2. Highlight one acorn with a red circle #FF3333 representing an individual measurement. 3. Display a group of acorns labeled 'Sample' appearing in a box. 4. Animate the 'average' weight calculation shifting from a single acorn to a group. 5. Show the Squirrel looking confused at individual data but relieved at group data.
1. Initialize with an irregular population distribution shape #FF5733. 2. Show 5, 10, 20, 30 samples drawn from the population. 3. Plot each sample mean as a new dot on an emerging curve. 4. Animate the curve smoothing from irregular to a bell shape #33FF57 as n increases. 5. Use a color transition from #FF5733 to #33FF57 to indicate the convergence.
1. Display 'n=5' text in red #FF3333 showing a jagged curve. 2. Show 'n=30' text in green #33FF57 showing a smooth Bell Curve. 3. Animate a 'Scale of Stability' bar increasing in width as n grows. 4. Highlight the Bell Curve apex in yellow #FFFF33. 5. Final display of 'Central Limit Theorem' title in white #FFFFFF.
1. Display a conveyor belt of lightbulbs with a 'Robot' arm. 2. Show 'Confidence Interval' brackets #33FFFF around the mean. 3. Draw a Z-score calculation on the side in #FFFFFF. 4. Show the bridge between the sample box and the massive population. 5. Final summary screen with 'CLT' glowing in #FFFFFF.

Section: section_2 — The Core Problem: Why Sample Means?

Lecture lines:
We often need population parameters.
Surveying everyone is impossible.
Sample means reveal order in chaos.

Planned animations:
1. Show an acorn icon popping up into the scene. 2. Highlight one acorn with a red circle #FF3333 representing an individual measurement. 3. Display a group of acorns labeled 'Sample' appearing in a box. 4. Animate the 'average' weight calculation shifting from a single acorn to a group. 5. Show the Squirrel looking confused at individual data but relieved at group data.
1. Show a 'Population' box full of varied acorns. 2. Highlight random selection of 5 acorns with a highlight color #FFFF33. 3. Draw a line from the selection to an 'Average' calculation panel. 4. Animate the result appearing on a graph. 5. Emphasize the shift from individual erratic values to consistent sample means.
1. Depict a large forest background. 2. Show the Survey Squirrel running between many acorn piles. 3. Animate a 'Total Mean' calculation. 4. Highlight the efficiency gain of sample means over measuring every acorn. 5. Transition to a summary label 'Population Estimation' in white #FFFFFF.

Section: section_3 — The CLT Mechanism (Visual Experiment)

Lecture lines:
Pick many samples from a population.
Calculate the mean for each sample.
Plotting these means forms a pattern.
The shape becomes a bell curve.
Larger samples make the curve precise.

Planned animations:
1. Initialize with an irregular population distribution shape #FF5733. 2. Show 5, 10, 20, 30 samples drawn from the population. 3. Plot each sample mean as a new dot on an emerging curve. 4. Animate the curve smoothing from irregular to a bell shape #33FF57 as n increases. 5. Use a color transition from #FF5733 to #33FF57 to indicate the convergence.
1. Show 1000 'Survey Squirrel' trials in a rapid animation loop. 2. Each trial plots a dot at the mean weight. 3. Accumulate dots to form a central pile. 4. Animate the pile rising into a distinct Bell Curve. 5. Highlight the final Bell Curve apex with #FFFF33.
1. Display the 'Population' icon #FF5733 shrinking. 2. Show the 'Bell Curve' result #33FF57 growing. 3. Animate a transformation line connecting the two. 4. Label the transition 'CLT Effect'. 5. Finalize by fading in white #FFFFFF text for 'Convergence'.
1. Highlight the sampling process with flashing borders #33FFFF. 2. Animate the mean calculations moving towards the central axis. 3. Display numerical progression for sample means. 4. Emphasize the distribution of means rather than individual points. 5. Show the resulting curve centered perfectly.
1. Summarize the process with a flow chart: Samples -> Means -> Bell Curve. 2. Use directional arrows #FFFFFF indicating the flow. 3. Highlight the final output 'Normal Distribution'. 4. Animate a 'Success' checkmark icon. 5. Fade out all elements except the final curve.

Section: section_4 — Critical Knowledge Points

Lecture lines:
Sample means always approach normality.
Original distribution shape doesn't matter.
Sample size thirty ensures significance.

Planned animations:
1. Display 'n=5' text in red #FF3333 showing a jagged curve. 2. Show 'n=30' text in green #33FF57 showing a smooth Bell Curve. 3. Animate a 'Scale of Stability' bar increasing in width as n grows. 4. Highlight the Bell Curve apex in yellow #FFFF33. 5. Final display of 'Central Limit Theorem' title in white #FFFFFF.
1. Draw a horizontal axis labeled 'Sample Size'. 2. Show the curve shape change dynamically as n moves from 2 to 30. 3. Flash 'n >= 30' in white text #FFFFFF to emphasize the rule. 4. Highlight the threshold transition point. 5. Show 'Statistically Significant' label next to the curve.
1. Present a comparative display: 'Uniform Distribution', 'Exponential Distribution', and 'Skewed Distribution'. 2. Show each evolving into a Normal distribution at n=30. 3. Highlight the common result: Bell Curve. 4. Emphasize that the start shape is irrelevant. 5. Finalize with 'Universality' label in #FFFFFF.

Section: section_5 — Real-World Application & Summary

Lecture lines:
CLT bridges probability and statistics.
We infer populations from small samples.
It is the backbone of inference.

Planned animations:
1. Display a conveyor belt of lightbulbs with a 'Robot' arm. 2. Show 'Confidence Interval' brackets #33FFFF around the mean. 3. Draw a Z-score calculation on the side in #FFFFFF. 4. Show the bridge between the sample box and the massive population. 5. Final summary screen with 'CLT' glowing in #FFFFFF.
1. Show the 'Confidence Interval' formula expanding. 2. Highlight variables within the formula using distinct colors. 3. Animate the 'Population Mean' being estimated. 4. Show the interval narrowing as precision increases. 5. Emphasize reliability with a steady glow #33FFFF.
1. Present a final summary of the bridge concept. 2. Show CLT label centrally placed. 3. Use connecting lines to 'Samples' and 'Population' components. 4. Highlight the concept of 'Inference' with a sparkle effect. 5. End with the video title on a clean background.

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application & Summary", [
            "CLT bridges probability and statistics.", 
            "We infer populations from small samples.", 
            "It is the backbone of inference."
        ])

        conveyor = Line(start=self.grid["F2"], end=self.grid["F6"], color=GRAY)
        bulb = Circle(radius=0.2, color=YELLOW, fill_opacity=0.8)
        
        # 2. Bridge / Confidence Interval
        bridge = VGroup(
            Line(self.grid["D2"], self.grid["D6"], color=WHITE),
            Text("Population", font_size=18).move_to(self.grid["E4"]),
            Text("Sample", font_size=18).move_to(self.grid["C4"])
        )
        ci_bracket = Brace(Line(self.grid["C2"], self.grid["C6"]), color="#33FFFF")
        ci_text = ci_bracket.get_text("Confidence Interval").scale(0.8).set_color("#33FFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(BLUE)
        self.add(conveyor)
        self.play(FadeIn(bulb), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(bridge), FadeIn(ci_bracket), FadeIn(ci_text), run_time=2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(BLUE)
        formula = MathTex(r"\bar{x} \pm z \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}", font_size=32)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B3")
        self.play(Write(formula), run_time=2)
        self.play(Indicate(ci_bracket), run_time=1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(BLUE)
        final_label = Text("CLT: The Bridge", font_size=36, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(final_label, "A3")
        self.play(FadeIn(final_label), run_time=1)
        self.play(final_label.animate.set_color("#FFFFFF").scale(1.2), run_time=1)
        self.wait(2)
